# Task-Based Execution Model {#sec-task-execution}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A query plan is a static description of what to compute. A
running query is the dynamic process of computing it. The bridge
between the two is the execution model: how operators get scheduled,
how state is held while operators run, how the lifecycle of a
query is managed.

NebulaStream's execution model is task-based. Every unit of work —
processing a `TupleBuffer`, starting a pipeline, stopping a source,
firing a window — is a typed `Task`. Worker threads consume tasks
from the queue (Chapter 15), execute them, and emit follow-up
tasks. There is no separate control plane; lifecycle and data flow
share the same queue.

This chapter walks through the data structures: `ExecutableQueryPlan`,
`RunningQueryPlan`, `RunningSource`, the `Task` variant. We have
already met the queue in Chapter 15; now we look at what it
schedules.

---

## 14.1 The lifetime of a query: three states {#sec-query-states}

A query passes through three states inside the engine:

**Compiled.** A `CompiledQueryPlan` is the artefact produced by
the compile pipeline (Chapter 11). It is a passive description:
function pointers, source descriptors, sink descriptors. Nothing
runs yet.

**Executable.** When the engine accepts a `CompiledQueryPlan`, it
constructs an `ExecutableQueryPlan` from it. The executable wraps
the compiled stages with runtime context: per-pipeline operator
handlers, callbacks for completion, identifiers. Still passive,
but ready to be started.

**Running.** When the user (or the engine's auto-start logic)
asks the engine to start the query, the executable becomes a
`RunningQueryPlan` plus per-pipeline `RunningQueryPlanNode`s plus
per-source `RunningSource`s. The sources begin emitting `WorkTask`s.
The query is alive.

These states are not just naming conventions. They correspond to
distinct types in `nes-query-engine/`:

```
CompiledQueryPlan        # nes-executable/
  ↓ (engine.registerQuery)
ExecutableQueryPlan      # nes-query-engine/
  ↓ (engine.startQuery)
RunningQueryPlan         # nes-query-engine/RunningQueryPlan.hpp
  + RunningQueryPlanNode # one per pipeline
  + RunningSource        # one per physical source
```

The transitions are explicit `StartQueryTask` and `StopQueryTask`
operations, scheduled through the same task queue as data work.

---

## 14.2 The Task variant {#sec-task-variant-revisited}

The full task variant lives in `nes-query-engine/Task.hpp`. We saw
it in Chapter 15:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/Task.hpp
using Task = std::variant<
    WorkTask,
    StopQueryTask,
    StartQueryTask,
    FailSourceTask,
    StopSourceTask,
    PendingPipelineStopTask,
    StopPipelineTask,
    StartPipelineTask>;
```

Eight kinds of task. Two kinds of work: data (`WorkTask`) and
lifecycle (the rest). Worker threads dispatch on the variant via
`std::visit`:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/QueryEngine.cpp (sketch)
void handleTask(Task task)
{
    std::visit([&](auto& concrete) {
        runHandler(concrete);
    }, task);
}
```

Each task type has a dedicated handler. `WorkTask` handlers call
the compiled pipeline's function pointer with the buffer; lifecycle
handlers consult the query catalog and adjust the running state.

The variant pattern means there is no virtual dispatch in the task
hierarchy itself — the dispatch is a `std::visit` jump table — and
every task type is type-checked at compile time. Adding a new task
type is adding a member to the variant and writing one handler.

---

## 14.3 RunningQueryPlanNode: pipelines as runtime objects {#sec-rqpn}

The runtime counterpart of a pipeline is a `RunningQueryPlanNode`,
defined in `nes-query-engine/RunningQueryPlan.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/RunningQueryPlan.hpp (sketch)
struct RunningQueryPlanNode {
    PipelineId id;
    std::atomic_bool requiresTermination = false;
    std::atomic<ssize_t> pendingTasks = 0;
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<RunningQueryPlanNode>> successors;
    std::unique_ptr<ExecutablePipelineStage> stage;
    std::function<void(Exception)> unregisterWithError;
    CallbackRef planRef;
    void fail(Exception exception) const {
        unregisterWithError(std::move(exception));
    }
};
```

Five fields deserve attention.

**`pendingTasks`** is the count of in-flight `WorkTask`s
referring to this pipeline. The `PendingPipelineStop` machinery
from Chapter 15 polls this count to decide when a pipeline can
be torn down.

**`requiresTermination`** is a flag flipped on after the pipeline's
setup phase completes. It tells the *deleter* (next paragraph)
whether to emit a stop task when the node's reference count
reaches zero. Setup-incomplete nodes can be deleted directly;
setup-complete nodes must shut down gracefully.

**`successors`** holds `shared_ptr`s to downstream nodes. This
is the engine's reference graph: a parent node keeps its
children alive. When a parent is dropped, the children's
reference count decrements and (potentially) the cascade
continues.

**`stage`** is the compiled function (Chapter 11), held by
`unique_ptr` because the pipeline node has exclusive ownership.

**`unregisterWithError`** is the failure callback, captured at
construction. `node.fail(exception)` invokes it; the callback
reports up to the query lifetime listener and tears the query
plan down.

The reference-count machinery uses a custom deleter, not C++'s
default `delete`:

```cpp
// nes-query-engine/RunningQueryPlan.cpp (sketch)
struct RunningQueryPlanNodeDeleter {
    WorkEmitter& emitter;
    QueryId queryId;
    void operator()(RunningQueryPlanNode* node) const noexcept {
        if (node->requiresTermination.load()) {
            emitter.emitPipelineStop(queryId, std::unique_ptr<RunningQueryPlanNode>(node));
        } else {
            delete node;
        }
    }
};

std::shared_ptr<RunningQueryPlanNode> RunningQueryPlanNode::create(
    QueryId queryId, PipelineId pipelineId, WorkEmitter& emitter,
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<RunningQueryPlanNode>> successors,
    std::unique_ptr<ExecutablePipelineStage> stage,
    std::function<void(Exception)> unregisterWithError,
    CallbackRef planRef, CallbackRef setupCallback)
{
    auto node = std::shared_ptr<RunningQueryPlanNode>(
        new RunningQueryPlanNode(pipelineId, std::move(successors),
                                 std::move(stage), std::move(unregisterWithError),
                                 std::move(planRef)),
        RunningQueryPlanNodeDeleter{.emitter = emitter, .queryId = queryId});
    emitter.emitPipelineStart(queryId, node, std::move(setupCallback));
    return node;
}
```

When the last `shared_ptr` to a node is dropped, the deleter
runs. If the node's setup completed (`requiresTermination ==
true`), the deleter emits a `PipelineStop` task and *transfers
ownership* of the raw pointer into a `unique_ptr` inside the
task. The pipeline gets torn down asynchronously, on a worker
thread, through the same task queue that processes data.

Tasks reference pipelines through `weak_ptr`. A worker about to
process a `WorkTask` first locks the `weak_ptr` to a `shared_ptr`;
if the lock fails (the pipeline has been destroyed under us), the
task is dropped. This is the engine's primary defence against
use-after-free across worker threads, and it is the reason the
custom deleter must transfer ownership through a task rather
than tearing down inline — by the time the deleter runs, other
worker threads may still hold weak_ptrs that they expect to
locate cleanly.

---

## 14.4 RunningSource: a source instance lifecycle {#sec-running-source}

The runtime counterpart of a `Source` (Chapter 8) is a
`RunningSource`, in `nes-query-engine/RunningSource.hpp`. The
`RunningSource` wraps a `SourceHandle` (the constructed source
instance) and manages its lifecycle:

- **Start.** A worker thread accepts a `StartPipelineTask` for the
  source's source-pipeline; the running source begins reading
  from its underlying source (`fillTupleBuffer`) and emitting
  `WorkTask`s into the admission queue.
- **Stop.** A `StopSourceTask` triggers a graceful shutdown. The
  source stops reading; in-flight buffers continue to flow.
- **Fail.** A `FailSourceTask` arrives if the source raises an
  exception (e.g., the file disappears, the TCP connection
  resets). The source is torn down; the query catalog is notified.

`RunningSource` has its own state machine. Sources can be
`STARTING`, `RUNNING`, `STOPPING`, `STOPPED`. The transitions are
serialised through the same task queue, ensuring that a source
cannot, for example, attempt to emit a `WorkTask` while it is
mid-shutdown.

---

## 14.5 The NodeEngine: the bridge between compiled plan and runtime {#sec-node-engine}

A small but important module we have not yet pinned down:
`nes-runtime/`. It provides the `NodeEngine` class — the
single object that owns the per-worker runtime context. Its
job is to bridge from the compile pipeline's output (a
`CompiledQueryPlan`) to the worker's execution machinery (the
two-queue scheduler, the buffer pool, the source registry).

Concretely, `NodeEngine` exposes:

```cpp
// nes-runtime/include/NodeEngine.hpp (sketch)
class NodeEngine {
public:
    void registerQuery(std::unique_ptr<CompiledQueryPlan> plan);
    void startQuery(QueryId id);
    void stopQuery(QueryId id);
    QueryStatus queryStatus(QueryId id) const;
    // ...
};
```

This is also where the `nes-executable/` module's
`CompiledQueryPlan` lives, structurally:

```cpp
// nes-executable/include/CompiledQueryPlan.hpp (sketch)
struct CompiledQueryPlan {
    QueryId id;
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<ExecutablePipeline>> pipelines;
    std::vector<SourceDescriptor> sources;
    std::vector<SinkDescriptor> sinks;
};

class ExecutablePipeline {
    PipelineId id;
    std::unique_ptr<ExecutablePipelineStage> stage;
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<ExecutablePipeline>> successors;
};
```

The `ExecutablePipelineStage` is the abstract interface that
the JIT (Chapter 12) implements; `CompiledExecutablePipelineStage`
is the concrete subclass holding the function pointer.
`PipelineExecutionContext` (also in `nes-runtime/`) carries the
per-pipeline runtime state — buffer providers, listeners — that
operators consult during execution.

The takeaway: `nes-executable/` defines the *shape* of a
compiled query; `nes-runtime/` defines the *engine* that runs
it. The query engine module (`nes-query-engine/`) holds the
scheduler that schedules its tasks. The three modules are
distinct because their lifetimes are different: a
`CompiledQueryPlan` outlives any individual run; the
`NodeEngine` lives for the worker's lifetime; the query engine's
schedulable tasks come and go per buffer.

## 14.6 Worker threads, work emitters, lifetime controllers {#sec-worker-interfaces}

The worker side of the engine has two interfaces, in
`nes-query-engine/Interfaces.hpp`:

- **`WorkEmitter`** — the abstract interface a worker uses to
  emit a follow-up task. The implementation is the engine's
  internal queue; the interface keeps the worker decoupled from
  the queue type. (This is the same interface that makes it easy
  to mock the queue for tests.)
- **`QueryLifetimeController`** — the abstract interface for
  lifecycle changes (start, stop, fail). Concrete implementations
  push tasks into the queue.

These interfaces give the worker a small, stable contract. The
worker does not know that it is using two folly queues; it knows
that there is something it can put work into and something it can
ask about query lifetime.

---

## 14.6 Putting it together: a tuple's journey {#sec-tuple-journey}

To pull all these threads together, here is the journey of a
single tuple through the running engine, from source to sink:

1. A `RunningSource` for source `demo` calls
   `Source::fillTupleBuffer` and gets back an 8 KiB buffer with,
   say, 1024 tuples.
2. The running source wraps the buffer in a `WorkTask` and writes
   it to the admission queue via `WorkEmitter::emit`.
3. A worker thread dequeues the `WorkTask`. It is for pipeline 1
   (the source pipeline).
4. The worker locks the weak_ptr in the task to the
   `RunningQueryPlanNode` for pipeline 1. Increments
   `pendingTasks`.
5. The worker invokes the compiled function pointer for pipeline 1
   on the buffer. The function loops over the 1024 tuples,
   processes each (in our demo: identity projection), and writes
   them to the sink's output formatter.
6. As tuples are processed, the compiled code emits one or more
   follow-up `WorkTask`s if the pipeline has downstream consumers
   beyond the sink. (For our demo, there are no downstreams; the
   sink is the end.)
7. The function returns. The worker decrements `pendingTasks`.
8. If the buffer originated as a source emission, the source's
   completion callback runs.

Steps 1–8 typically execute in microseconds for a small buffer.
The queue, the weak_ptr lock, and the function call together add
on the order of 100 ns of overhead per buffer; the rest is
operator work.

In a distributed deployment (Chapter 19), one further step is
inserted at any pipeline boundary that crosses a worker: a
`NetworkSink` serialises the buffer onto a Rust-side channel,
and a `NetworkSource` deserialises it on the other side. From
the worker's point of view the network sink/source pair looks
identical to any other sink/source pair; the data plane between
workers is the only piece that knows it is crossing a network.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch14-summary}

The execution model is task-based and unified: data work and
lifecycle work share a single typed `Task` variant, dispatched
through `std::visit`. Pipelines are runtime objects
(`RunningQueryPlanNode`) with reference counts that gate graceful
shutdown. Sources are wrapped in `RunningSource` instances with
their own state machines. Worker threads use small abstract
interfaces (`WorkEmitter`, `QueryLifetimeController`) that decouple
them from the queue and lifecycle implementation. The combination
gives the engine a uniform model: every action is a task; every
worker is a task processor.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch14-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 14.1: count tasks"}
Run a join systest in TRACE mode. Count the number of each task
variant produced over the test's lifetime. The ratio
`WorkTask : lifecycle tasks` will be very large; that is the
right thing to see.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 14.2: trace a stop"}
Submit a query, let it run for a few seconds, then stop it via
`nes-repl`. In TRACE logs, find the sequence of `StopQueryTask`,
`StopSourceTask`, `StopPipelineTask`, `PendingPipelineStopTask`.
What is the order? Which tasks are emitted from the admission
queue, which from the internal queue?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 14.3: weak_ptr in action"}
Add an `NES_DEBUG` log inside the worker's `lock()` of the
`weak_ptr` in `WorkTask`. Force a query stop while traffic is
in flight. You should see the lock occasionally fail (returning
nullptr) for tasks that arrived after the pipeline was torn
down. The dropped tasks are silently ignored.
:::
